title: Strategies to Increase Adherence. Active Physical Education for Life
summary:
Adherence is the degree to which a woman consistently, voluntarily and with motivation follows the prescribed activity. In pregnancy it is challenged by physical and hormonal changes, fatigue, nausea, fear, lack of time and lack of support, so it has to be approached as active physical education for life and not only as training design.

The chapter reviews behavior models, barriers and facilitators, and individual, social and programmatic determinants. Strategies include education, motivational communication, SMART goals, group exercise, flexibility, professional supervision and technology. It also offers profile-specific advice, ways to measure adherence, and evidence of the benefits of high adherence.
points: Barriers are physical (nausea, fatigue, back pain), psychological (fear of harming the baby), social, cultural and economic or logistical.
Self-efficacy is one of the strongest predictors of behavioral commitment.
SMART goals are Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound, for example increasing walking from 20 to 30 minutes daily in four weeks.
Supervised group programs achieve adherence rates exceeding 80%, compared with less than 40% in individual home-based programs.
Offering Option A (in-person) and Option B (online) for the day's training prevents dropout when a full session is not possible.
Supervision by a trained specialist is one of the strongest predictors of adherence.
Digital platforms double the continuity of exercise at home during pregnancy.
Women active during pregnancy are up to four times more likely to remain active postpartum.
High adherence to supervised programs reduces gestational diabetes risk by 45%, gestational hypertension by 38% and cesarean likelihood by 25%.
takeaways: Set SMART goals and track them in a log, chart or app.
Exercise with a group or build a support network, such as a chat group, to stay motivated.
Keep a backup plan, such as an online version, for low-energy days.
Learn self-monitoring tools like the Borg scale and talk test and the warning signs.
Focus on how you feel (energy, mood, less pain) rather than on physical results.
Sedentary women should start with small goals and gentle exercises; athletes should redefine goals as intensity drops.
Track attendance weekly, and participation and satisfaction quarterly.
cautions: Technology must be complemented by professional supervision to ensure safety and appropriate intensity.
